# CHANGELOG

Completed features, fixes, enhancements, security fixes, and released changes.

**Classification (Code Review SOP, CODE_REVIEW_PROMPT.md v1.0, Phase 10):** this
file records **completed work only**. All outstanding work, including
owner-gated work, is a GitHub issue (owner decision 2026-09-05; `TODO.md` keeps
the accepted risks and an index to the issues); required-input references and
formats belong in [Required-Inputs](docs/standards/required-inputs.md). `REVIEW.md` was
retired on 2026-08-29 and must not be recreated.

Format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).
This project has not cut a tagged release; entries are grouped under
`[Unreleased]` and reference the pull request that landed them.

## [Unreleased]

### Features

- **The visitor session broker's Coder token, `CODER_BROKER_TOKEN`, is now declared in Terraform as a Key Vault reference to the secret `CODER-BROKER-TOKEN`, the way every other credential the Function App reads is (the declaration half of arming the sweep timer; follow-up to item 1 of [#1403](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1403)) ([pull request](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1422)).** The code had read `CODER_BROKER_TOKEN` since the visitor sessions were built, but nothing in `infra/` declared it, so a copy set by hand would have been removed by the next apply, and switching the sweep timer on would have done nothing useful. `infra/functionapp.tf` gains the reference. `functions/src/lib/secret-catalog.js` lists it, so the Integrations → Keys page offers it in the Labs group, and `functions/src/lib/credentials/register.js` registers it as a hand-rotated credential with no rotation rule yet. `scripts/check-unresolved-secrets.mjs` lists it as expected-unresolved until the owner seeds it (the cap in its test moves from 5 to 6), and `scripts/assert-expected-plan.mjs` declares the new app setting so `tfc-plan-check` reads the plan as `DECLARED`. While the secret does not exist the app behaves as it did before: the broker reads the token as not set, so a session cannot start (the visitor routes answer `VISITOR_NOT_CONFIGURED` once `LABS_VISITOR_SESSIONS_ENABLED` is on and Turnstile is seeded), and the timer logs one Warning and calls nothing; applying the reference first is safe because Terraform writes only the reference and never reads the vault. New tests tie the setting names the code reads (`CODER_BROKER_TOKEN_SETTING`, `TURNSTILE_SECRET_SETTING`) to the references in `infra/` and fail when the broker's reference is removed. Documentation: [Required inputs](docs/standards/required-inputs.md) §4.1 (the `enabled_timers` row now says plainly that the timer keeps cleaning up existing sessions while `LABS_VISITOR_SESSIONS_ENABLED` is off, the wording point CodeRabbit raised on #1412), §4.5 and §4.6; [Variables and secrets](docs/standards/variables-and-secrets.md) (32 references); the [lab host runbook](docs/runbooks/labs-host.md) ("Arming it" step 1 and the new "Seeding the broker token", with how to take it away again); ADR 0032's amendment; the cold rebuild list; the rotation schedule and the compromise tiers. Still open in #1403 and not done here: which Coder user and permissions the token is made with (item 4), and `LABS_VISITOR_SESSIONS_ENABLED`, which `infra/` still does not declare. Nothing was applied or run against Azure, HCP Terraform or Coder.
- **A timer, `sweepVisitorSessions`, runs the visitor lab session sweep every two minutes on its own, so a Coder clean-up that Coder has not confirmed no longer waits for the next visitor (item 1 of [#1403](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1403); the owner answered `timer`) ([pull request](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1412)).** `reapExpiredVisitorSessions` ends visitor lab sessions past their hour and retries the clean-ups of the workspace and user that Coder has not yet confirmed ([#1388](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1388)). It ran only when a visitor read the lab's status or started a session, so with no visitors, or with `LABS_VISITOR_SESSIONS_ENABLED` off (the status route answers before it sweeps), a waiting session, and the Coder user and host workspace slot it held, waited. The new timer (`functions/src/functions/visitor-session-sweep.js`, one run in `functions/src/lib/timers/visitor-session-sweep.js`) calls the same sweep with the real store, `fetch` and `readBrokerConfig`. **Why every two minutes:** a refused clean-up is tried again after 2, 4, 6 and 8 minutes, a dead claim is taken over after 5 and a session lasts 60, so two minutes puts each retry within one tick of being due (five minutes would turn the 2-minute retry into a 5-minute one; one minute would double the runs, because a visitor's own request already runs the sweep at most once a minute). A run with nothing to do is three queries on `lab_jobs` and no call to Coder, about 2,160 queries a day; request-unit cost was not measured against the live account. **It is bounded:** at most 10 sessions a run (`MAX_SWEEP_SESSIONS`) and a 10-second limit on each Coder call. **It never creates a session or a Coder user:** it is given only the query, read and conditional-replace operations, a test watches every operation that would create or overwrite a document, and the only thing it asks Coder to build is a workspace delete. **It runs whatever `LABS_VISITOR_SESSIONS_ENABLED` says**, because that switch closes the door to new visitors and turning it off while sessions exist must not strand their Coder users and workspaces. **It does nothing at all, not even a query, when Coder is not set up** (`CODER_URL` and `CODER_BROKER_TOKEN`; `readBrokerConfig` no longer falls back to the read-only status token, which cannot delete anything): the sweep would otherwise spend one of a waiting session's five tries on every tick, and five tries end a session as `cleanup_failed`. **It logs counts and kinds only** (`reaped`, `finished`, `pending`, `failed`; the kind of an error; never a session, a Coder id, or any text Coder or Cosmos sent), as a Warning when the run did something and as Information otherwise (`host.json` ships only Warning), and **it never throws out of the handler**: a failed run is one Warning line and the next tick tries again. Because a run that cannot sweep still counts as a success to `alert-timer-overdue`, the runbook says to look for that Warning. **The trade-off:** before the timer, tries were spent only when a visitor arrived; now they are spent on the clock (at about 0, 2, 6, 12 and 20 minutes, a retry slipping a tick when a run starts late), so a Coder or token outage longer than about twenty to thirty minutes leaves the waiting sessions as `cleanup_failed`, for a person to finish by hand. No alert reads those lines yet; that is in #1403. **Two runs at once cannot double-call Coder:** the Functions host runs one copy of a timer across all instances and does not start it while a run is still going ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-functions/functions-bindings-timer#usage)), and, without relying on that, the sweep claims a session with a conditional write before it calls Coder; tests run two timer runs, and a timer run with a visitor's sweep, at the same moment and count the Coder calls. One limit: a claim lasts 5 minutes from the start of a sweep, and ten sessions whose Coder calls all run to their 10-second limit can use all of it, so a claim taken over then can lead to a second, harmless delete (Coder answers 404 or 410 for what is gone) that spends one try; the margin is an open item in #1403. The sweep in the visitors' requests stays, with its once-a-minute limit, as the only sweep while the timer is off. **Hardened in the same change, because the timer runs unattended with the broker's token:** `readBrokerConfig` no longer falls back to the read-only status token (every create and delete with it would be refused, and each refused clean-up try is spent), so without `CODER_BROKER_TOKEN` the broker is not configured; an id or name saved in a session record is written into a Coder URL only when it is plainly an id (not `..`, nothing with a slash, `?`, `#` or `%`, and not `me`, which Coder reads as the caller's own account); a record's own `endStatus` and try count are read only when they are one of the two final statuses and a whole number; and a log line names an error only by its status, system code or class. **Infrastructure (plan only, nothing applied from here):** the flag `SWEEP_VISITOR_SESSIONS` joins `local.timer_catalogue` (`infra/functionapp.tf`) and the `enabled_timers` allowlist (`infra/variables.tf`), so the Function App gains `FEATURE_FLAG_SWEEP_VISITOR_SESSIONS = "false"`, off until the owner adds the name to `enabled_timers`; `sweepVisitorSessions` joins `local.timer_schedules` (`infra/observability.tf`), so `alert-timer-overdue` watches it; and `scripts/assert-expected-plan.mjs` declares both changes for the plan check, in each state the alert's timer list can be in. Registered in `functions/src/functions/index.js`, `function-inventory.json`, the registration-shim list and the route inventory (now 29 timers). The runbook (`docs/runbooks/labs-host.md`, "The sweep timer") says what to check, how to arm it, and how to turn it off or roll it back; ADR 0032 (a dated amendment), `.azure/api-surface.json` and `docs/standards/required-inputs.md` say it too. `docs/standards/required-inputs.md` also records that `CODER_BROKER_TOKEN` is declared nowhere in `infra/` (**MISSING**), so a copy set by hand would be removed by the next apply: declaring it is its own change, tracked in #1403. Tests fail on the tree without the timer (6 of the 7 timer test files), on the lab sweep code as it was before the hardening (25 tests), and on 38 hand-made changes, all caught, among them: the timer not registered, the gate inverted, the schedule changed, an error let out of the handler, `createDoc` handed to the sweep, the master switch ignored, the sweep waiting for the visitor-session switch, a run that logs the broker token or the error text, a run that sweeps with no Coder settings or with only the status token, a path that takes `..` or `me`, and each of the infrastructure and plan-check edits left out. What is still open in #1403 (items 2 to 9, and the new items found while building this: a time-based try budget, an alert on the Warning lines, the lease measured from the start of a sweep) stays there. Not live until the owner has merged, applied the Terraform run, deployed the functions, declared `CODER_BROKER_TOKEN` in Terraform (it is not today) and added `SWEEP_VISITOR_SESSIONS` to `enabled_timers`; nothing here was applied or run against live Azure, Coder or Cosmos.

- **Second Brain is implemented inside HCW admin ([#1395](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1395)).** The owner-only workspace connects private Markdown notes, revisions, topics/projects, creator references, search and a keyboard-accessible map. Existing editors can capture research and create reviewed drafts with private provenance. An on-demand Foundry assistant cites workspace sources. The Windows Obsidian companion uses a dedicated `brain_sync` client, encrypted token storage and recoverable conflicts. Private records join authored backups; indexes can be rebuilt. Deployment starts with both feature flags off, with owner configuration and real-vault enrollment governed by the [rollout runbook](docs/runbooks/second-brain.md).
- **The website now counts the lab sessions it starts for visitors, and the Labs hub Dashboard has a card that shows the count (editors and admins only; nothing public).** Each time the visitor session broker creates a new session (`functions/src/lib/labs/visitor-session.js`), it adds one to a per-lab, per-UTC-day tally (`functions/src/lib/labs/lab-starts.js`): one `lab-starts:YYYY-MM-DD` document `{ day, total, byLab }` and one `lab-starts:meta` marker `{ since }` in the `system` container, each written only if nobody else changed it since it was read (an ETag check), so two overlapping starts do not lose a count. The counting documents hold nothing that identifies a person (no IP address, client key, session id, user id, token, query string or time of day), and `lab-starts.test.js` fails if a stored document gains any other key. A repeat request that returns a live session, a page view, a refused request and a failed provision are not counted; a counter fault is logged by code only and never reaches the visitor. New editor route `GET cms/labs/starts` (`cmsLabsStarts`) returns today, the last 7 days, the last 30 days, the total and a per-lab breakdown; the card shows them with the day counting began, says in plain words that it counts sessions and not people, and has **Copy as text for a letter**, which writes one plain sentence with the real numbers and the date range (no vendor names). Counting is on from the deploy: the visitor session records are deleted about two hours after their last update, so there is no earlier history and none is estimated. Signed-in member starts inside the lab pane and the public validation runs are not visitor sessions and are not counted. The broker's lab check now uses an own-property test, so ids such as `constructor` or `toString` are refused instead of passing. `docs/runbooks/labs-host.md` has the new "Counting lab starts" section. Not live until the functions and the frontend are deployed.
- **A standard and a fill-in dossier say what an open-source Docker app from Hybrid Cloud Works must look like to qualify for Docker's free open-source programme (DSOS), with Network Eyes as the worked example (ticket [#678](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/678)).** `docs/standards/oss-docker-app-dossier.md` quotes Docker's four rules from its programme and application pages (read 2026-10-25) and says what the pages leave out: whether an organisation that already pays for a Docker plan can be accepted, which the page tells the reader to ask Docker in writing. It lists thirteen checks (OSS-1 to OSS-13: public source and images, an OSI-approved licence with the same SPDX id in `LICENSE`, the Dockerfile label, `NOTICE` and the README, the copyright holder, OIDC-only publishing with provenance, an SBOM and a Scout check, the `img-<code>-<lab-addon|appliance-app>` name, no paid edition and no customer or client wording, active development, community files, the two rulesets, and Dependabot, CodeQL and dependency review), each with a PowerShell command and the result to expect, a template block to fill for the next product, and a short paragraph on moving a product to its own Docker organisation if it ever gets a paid edition. The Network Eyes example uses values read from the repository, Docker Hub and the registry on 2026-10-25 and 26. It records what [HCW-NetworkEyes_App#316](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-NetworkEyes_App/pull/316) fixed while the page was being written (the copyright holder in `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`, and the "client" and "customer" wording) and the gaps that remain on `main`: "lab edition" wording in the README and `CLAUDE.md`, no licence label on the lab add-on image, a stored Docker secret that no workflow uses, and a tag ruleset that lists the repository-admin role as a bypass actor. The page is registered in `mkdocs.yml` and linked from section 2.11 of the [field application standard](docs/standards/hcw-field-application-standard.md). No guard script was added, because this repository has no existing test that checks standards pages. Nothing was sent to Docker.

The `functions (azure)` row of `ci.yml` now watches all of `docs/content/` instead of the two contract files, so the guard also runs on a pull request that only adds such a file. `.claude/CLAUDE.md` gains "Pre-publish content never goes in this public repository", and the "why the notes stay outside" paragraph of `docs/runbooks/obsidian-idea-notes.md` names the guard. Checked by adding a `docs/content/blog-test.md`: the test failed with that message, then passed once the file was removed.

- **The idea-note promote script now saves a draft into the owner's private vault, never into the public repository (PR 2 of the move of pre-publish drafts out of the repository; owner rule 2026-10-25, follows [#1379](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1379)).** `scripts/ideas/promote-idea.mjs` wrote `docs/content/blog-<name>.md` into the working tree; it now writes `<vault>/Drafts/blog-<name>.md`, where the vault comes from `--vault <folder>` or the `HCW_VAULT` environment variable, and stops with a plain-language error (exit 2) when neither is given or the vault folder does not exist. `--out-dir` is removed. It refuses (exit 1, nothing written) any output folder that resolves inside the repository, whether given as a relative path, with `..`, in a different case on Windows or macOS, or through a symlink or junction (links are followed with the real path, and the comparison runs again after the folder is made). The file format is unchanged, and `functions/src/lib/cms/idea-promotion.test.js` still reads the output with `parseRepoDraft` and now also with `parseMarkdownDraft`, the reader behind the Admin → Drafts upload. New tests cover a path inside the repository, relative paths, `..` tricks, a junction and symlink into the repository, a link that points elsewhere, a missing vault and `HCW_VAULT`, and assert that no test run leaves a file under `docs/content` (they fail against the old script). `docs/runbooks/obsidian-idea-notes.md` is rewritten so the steps are promote into the vault `Drafts` folder, then upload on Admin → Drafts, with every instruction that sent a draft through a pull request removed and the reason explained; the Drafts stage section of `docs/content/blog-machine.md` now says the Drafts page is the source of truth and the import-from-repository route is being retired. Not removed here (a separate change): the 17 existing `docs/content` drafts, their mkdocs entries and the import route.
- **Admin → Drafts can take a whole markdown file, or several at once, straight from the owner's private vault, so a pre-publish draft no longer has to be committed to the public repository (PR 1 of the move; owner decision 2026-10-25).** `POST cms/drafts/from-markdown` takes `{ markdown, origin }` (`origin` is `vault` or `paste`) at the editor role, reads the text with the docs/content import's own parser (`parseRepoDraft`, which needs no repository path, so the import's path checks are untouched), checks it with the rules a typed draft goes through (`validateDraftFields`, 256 KB body cap, 272 KB for the whole file, the request body counted as it is read and abandoned past 545 KB, with or without a Content-Length) and writes a `drafting`, never-public draft with `draftOrigin` `vault` or `paste` (`functions/src/lib/cms/drafts-markdown.js`, `drafts-handlers.js`). The document id comes from the normalised title, so a second upload of the same article, even a double click, answers `ALREADY_IMPORTED` (with the stage it is at) instead of duplicating, and a title a published article already carries is skipped; a file that is not a draft is a 422 with the parser's reason. The markdown is never logged and never put in an audit row. The Drafts page gains a **Paste or upload a markdown draft** panel: a picker for many `.md` files sent one request at a time with a result line per file (created, already present, or the reason it was not added; one bad file does not stop the rest) and a closing total, plus a box for one pasted draft; the list labels drafts *From my vault* and *Pasted in*. Registered in the route inventory, `function-inventory.json`, `.azure/api-surface.json` and the client timeout table. The docs/content import is unchanged and stays until a later change retires it. `docs/runbooks/obsidian-idea-notes.md` and the Drafts stage section of `docs/content/blog-machine.md` describe the new path. Not yet live: the owner deploys the functions and the frontend, and the admin sign-in path is not exercised by tests.

- **Idea notes: an Obsidian second brain for content, with a format, a check and
  a promote-to-draft script (#1343)**. Owner request 2026-10-24. The vault lives
  on the owner's computer, outside this public repository; the scripts take its
  folder as an argument and only ever read it. An idea note is a note whose
  properties are `type`, `theme`, `format` and `status` (and optionally title,
  subtitle, tags, reading, part, date). `scripts/ideas/check-idea-notes.mjs
  <folder>` reports what is wrong with each note and a count by status and type.
  `scripts/ideas/promote-idea.mjs <note>` turns an `outlined` blog idea whose
  format is how-to or build-log into `docs/content/blog-<name>.md`, in the shape
  the admin's *Import from docs/content* takes; it never overwrites, never edits
  the note, and refuses what can only be private notes or only work in Obsidian
  (`[[wikilinks]]`, `%% comments %%`, Dataview and Tasks blocks). The properties
  are read by a small reader of our own, with no new dependency, because
  Obsidian writes lists in the block form and the import's reader takes only the
  inline form. Runbook: `docs/runbooks/obsidian-idea-notes.md`, written for
  someone who has never used Obsidian. Checked: 36 scripts tests on temporary
  vaults (never a real one); `functions/src/lib/cms/idea-promotion.test.js`
  reads each promoted draft back with the import's own parser (`parseRepoDraft`)
  and holds the format's limits and content types to the import's and the
  publisher's, seen failing when either was changed; the runbook's steps run
  once in PowerShell against a temporary vault, with the outputs it shows.
  `ci.yml`'s `functions` filter now names `scripts/ideas/idea-notes.mjs`. Not
  done: an admin screen for the backlog; promoting types other than blog; any
  look at the owner's real vault.

- **`go.hybridcloudworks.com` for the Linkie link-in-bio page**. Owner request
  2026-10-24. Linkie serves a custom hostname that CNAMEs to `app.linkie.bio`
  and proves ownership with a TXT record, both of which its Domain settings
  page lists once the name is saved there. `infra/frontend.tf` now declares the
  two records the way the podcast one is: a DNS-only CNAME `go`, and the TXT
  `_cf-custom-hostname.go` with the value Linkie generated. Declared as
  Terraform records, and not added by hand or through Cloudflare's API, so the
  daily Cloudflare DNS audit sees them as the workspace's own and the next
  plan shows no drift. Linkie's page also lists rows named `@` and `www`; it
  does not say whether those names are relative to `go` or to the zone, and
  read as the zone a CNAME at either would hand the site to Linkie, so only
  what its help article asks of a subdomain is declared: the CNAME and the TXT
  (an early draft of this entry, the runbook and the Terraform comment stated
  the zone reading as fact; it is unverified, and the wording now says so).
  The plan checker declared the two creates and the edge DNS runbook gains
  both rows and the `go` checks. Applied by the owner on 2026-10-24 (HCP
  Terraform status Success), after which both records answered on 1.1.1.1 and
  8.8.8.8 and the site's own apex and `www` were unchanged. The first browser
  request got Cloudflare error 1014 "CNAME Cross-User Banned", which
  Cloudflare's page says is how a cross-account CNAME answers until the target's
  owner (here Linkie) has registered the hostname with Cloudflare for SaaS. The
  declared creates are deleted from the plan checker. Linkie's status moves
  from Failed to Live when it has registered `go`, which its article says can
  take up to 48 hours.

- **A Telegram message when the delivery monitor goes red, and the monitor
  fires at 8 hours instead of 24**. Owner decision 2026-10-23. The
  "Monitor delivery health" check went red on 2026-10-22 because one line on
  a frontend page had waited more than a day for its by-hand deploy, and the
  only notice was GitHub's failure email. Now `checkAgentHealth` (the
  five-minute timer that is already running) reads that workflow's runs from
  GitHub's public API once an hour and sends one Telegram message titled
  "DELIVERY MONITOR RED", naming the job that failed and linking the run. A
  reminder goes again if it is still red a day later, and one "back to green"
  message follows when a run passes. If the bot cannot read GitHub 24 times
  in a row (about a day), it says so once, in a separate "WATCH IS BLIND"
  message, because a watch that has stopped reading looks the same as a
  green monitor. The repository is public, so this reads
  with no token: no GitHub secret was added, and the bot token stays in Key
  Vault. The cost is that it cannot speak while Azure is down; GitHub's own
  failure email still does. The threshold now lives only in
  `scripts/check-deploy-drift.mjs` (8 hours, was 24 there and again in the
  workflow). Functions need a deploy for the message to start; the threshold
  takes effect on merge.
  (`functions/src/lib/timers/delivery-monitor-watch.js`)

- **A monthly audience figure the site can state: a Cloudflare Web Analytics
  beacon at the edge and a monthly read into the Ambassador hub (#1302)**.
  Owner decision 2026-10-20: the Docker Captain application goes in on the
  Thought Leader track, which asks for 5,000 monthly views, and the Microsoft
  MVP form asks for impact metrics, so the site has to be able to state a
  monthly audience figure. Nothing is shown to visitors. `infra/frontend.tf`
  creates a Cloudflare Web Analytics site for `hybridcloudworks.com` with
  Cloudflare's lite option (no cookies, no client-side state, no
  fingerprinting; the option asks Cloudflare not to measure visitors in the
  EU, which Cloudflare documents for the snippet its proxy injects and which
  is unverified for the hand-placed one this site carries, so the figure is
  aggregate page views, read as a floor), counted on the new
  `cloudflare_account_id` workspace variable so that a plan without it stays
  whole, and the `cloudflare_api_token` gains Account → Account Settings →
  Write for the one account-level create. `web_analytics_site_token` and
  `web_analytics_site_tag` are outputs and not sensitive, because the token
  ships in every page. The frontend build
  (`frontend/scripts/cf-web-analytics.mjs`) puts the beacon before `</head>`
  only when `VITE_CF_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` is set — `deploy-azure-frontend.yml`
  reads it from the `CF_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repository variable — leaving
  `index.html` byte for byte unchanged without it and failing the build on a
  value that is not token-shaped; `connect-src` gains
  `https://cloudflareinsights.com`. The `ambassadorAudienceMonthly` timer
  runs daily at 06:45 UTC, because `alert-timer-overdue` cannot express a
  calendar month, and records the previous month once: page views from
  Cloudflare's GraphQL Analytics API with the read-only
  `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` (Account Analytics: Read, a second token and
  never the workspace's) and podcast downloads from Podbean through the
  existing client ("podcast downloads unavailable" in the row until that
  credential is seeded), as one `manual` evidence row per programme under
  Docker Captain's and Microsoft MVP's `reach` requirement, dated the last
  day of the month and idempotent by a deterministic id. Two riders: the
  footer carries a "GitKraken Ambassador" text link, and the Landing Zone
  Builder's credit reads "based on HashiCorp's validated pattern", the
  wording HashiCorp's trademark policy allows, with the pattern linked. The
  privacy policy names Cloudflare Web Analytics as a processor and says we
  have asked Cloudflare to exclude EU visitors, not that they are excluded.
  Owner steps, in order: add Account → Account Settings → Write to the
  `hcp-terraform-cloudflare-dns` token; set `cloudflare_account_id` on
  `hcw-azure` and apply; confirm the EU option on the new site's Manage page
  in the Web Analytics dashboard
  (`https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/web-analytics`) and record the
  date in the `cloudflare_account_id` row of required inputs §4.1; set
  `CF_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` from the `web_analytics_site_token` output and
  deploy the frontend; mint the
  read-only token and seed `CLOUDFLARE-ANALYTICS-TOKEN` on Integrations →
  Keys, then take `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` off `EXPECTED_UNRESOLVED` in
  `scripts/check-unresolved-secrets.mjs`; add `AMBASSADOR_AUDIENCE_MONTHLY` to
  `enabled_timers`. [Required inputs](docs/standards/required-inputs.md)
  §4.1, §4.2, §4.5, §4.6, §4.8 and §4.10 carry the rows.

- **Portainer read-only check on the lab host, reported into the Health Hub
  (#1282)**. The `portainer` role installs `hcw-portainer-check`: every 15
  minutes, and once on each `bootstrap.sh` run, it reads Portainer on the
  host's loopback with the owner's access token (`GET` only; the token root
  `0600`, handed to the unit through `LoadCredential`, never on a command

  licence dates to the site through the lab agent's new

  or its `local` environment is down, the check failed, or no report has

- **Visitor lab sessions: brokered ephemeral Coder workspaces for visitors outside the org (#1016)**.
  - Implemented `functions/src/lib/labs/visitor-session.js` to broker ephemeral Coder users (`v-<hex>`) and workspaces from template `hcw-lab` without granting permanent sign-up or accounts.
  - Enforced strict fail-closed constraints: origin lock against site apex/www, Cloudflare Turnstile token validation (`action: visitor-session`), per-client daily quota (2 sessions/day), global concurrency limit (`LABS_VISITOR_MAX_CONCURRENT=2`), and a 60-minute hard duration limit.
  - Added self-healing opportunistic reaper cleaning up expired workspaces and users from Coder and Cosmos DB `lab_jobs`.
  - Registered anonymous API endpoint `public/labs/visitor-session` supporting GET (status & active session), POST (start session), and DELETE (stop session), registered in `.azure/api-surface.json` and `functions/function-inventory.json`.
  - Updated frontend `publicApi.js` and `LabPanePage.jsx` to render visitor session controls with Turnstile verification, frame active visitor workspace URLs with an "End session" control, and display clear capacity notices when full.
- **A private "Doc Vault" in the admin, for the owner's own templates, applications and letters, kept apart from the Ambassador Evidence tab (owner request 2026-10-26).** `/admin/doc-vault` (Admin → Spotlight → Doc Vault, publisher and above) holds documents of six categories (Template, Application, Letter, Notes, Reference, Other) with tags (12 × 40), an optional https or `/admin/` link and up to 256 KB of plain text or markdown, shown exactly as written in a read-only box and never as a web page. Add by **Paste a document** or by **Upload files** (several `.md`, `.markdown`, `.txt` files, sent one at a time with a result line each; a failing file does not stop the rest; front matter `title`, `category`, `tags` including Obsidian's one-per-line form, and `link` are read, every other key is named in a warning and not kept). Each document has a **Copy** button (the text as saved) and **Copy as plain text** (without markdown marks), falling back to the older copy command where the clipboard is blocked. Adding a document with the same category and title as one already here is a **new version**, never a duplicate (identical text writes nothing); the newest ten versions are kept, each can be read and restored, and a restore is itself a new version. **Move to Trash** keeps a document and its history for 30 days (put back, or **Delete forever** from Trash), and the list load removes what is older. Nine routes under `cms/doc-vault` (`functions/src/lib/doc-vault/`), all at the **publisher** role, reads included: viewer is monitoring only, editor is the role an invited co-author holds, publisher is the first role trusted to put things in front of the public, which is the bar for the place that must stay out of it. Its own Cosmos container, `doc_vault` (`/id`, the text not indexed, no TTL; backed up as authored work, `infra/cosmos-containers.json`, the plan checker declares the one create), created by a Terraform apply that stays the owner's: until then every route answers 503 `NOT_PROVISIONED` and the page says the one step. Document ids are an HMAC of category and folded title under a salt item kept in the container, so an id in an audit row, a URL or telemetry cannot be checked against a guessed title. Every write and every read of a document writes a content-free audit row (id, version, category, source, size, admin id); text, title, tags and link never reach a log line, an audit row or an error, and answers are `Cache-Control: private, no-store`. Writes carry the etag of the version on screen (412 `CONFLICT` otherwise), the old text is archived before it is replaced, and a permanent delete marks the document `purging` before it removes anything so it cannot lose a live document's history or leave an orphan. Registered in `function-inventory.json`, `.azure/api-surface.json`, `route-inventory.test.js` (publisher on every route, not public), the client timeout table and the export classification. The byte-counting JSON body reader moved from `drafts-handlers.js` into `functions/src/lib/http/bounded-body.js` so both read a body the same way (behaviour unchanged, the Drafts tests pass). **Never public** is held by `functions/src/lib/doc-vault/no-leak.test.js`: no module outside the vault names the container, a vault document fails every public clause in every state, every public route run against a store that answers every read with a vault document serves none of it, and the page is under `/admin` only. A security review of the diff (the read-only `typescript-security-reviewer` agent) found no Critical or High issue; its six findings were acted on (salted ids, safe delete order, read auditing, no-store, backup wording, spell check off in the text box) except that the publisher role is shared by every publisher, which is stated in the runbook with the one-line change to `super_admin`. Checked: 259 new backend tests (four files under `functions/src/lib/doc-vault/`) and 99 new frontend tests, with the full suites green (functions 7,044 tests, frontend 5,444); mutation checks (19 deliberate breaks of the real code, each caught by the new tests, including a quadratic scan and a public-shape document) and the linear-time test failing on the first draft of the plain-text converter before its scan was bounded. `docs/runbooks/doc-vault.md` explains what goes here and what does not (and the difference from Evidence), who can use it and why, and the one-time setup. Not yet live: the container does not exist until the owner confirms the HCP Terraform run, the owner deploys the functions and the frontend, and the copy buttons were tested in a test browser, not in Edge, Chrome or Firefox on Windows.

- **Admin → Calendar: the owner's own dated alerts, on the existing Calendar page, with a pop-up on sign-in and the Docker-Sponsored Open Source application (due 2026-10-30) as the first ([#678](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/678)).** Owner request 2026-10-26, "Calendar Alerts when I log into the Admin portal", then "we already have a calendar in the admin portal so maybe we can build off of that": so there is no page or menu entry of its own. An alert is a title, a UTC day, an optional UTC time, an optional link (an https address or an `/admin/...` page) and a note of up to 500 characters; it is open, snoozed until a day, or done. **On the Calendar (`/admin/calendar`) an alert is an orange "Alert" chip with a bell on its due day** (a new kind `alert` in the `GET cms/calendar` read, one more collector in `COLLECTORS`, `functions/src/lib/calendar-alerts/collector.js`; same editor role, read-only, handed no write function), filterable with the toolbar's Kinds and Status; pressing it opens Done or Reopen, Snooze, Open link, Edit and Delete, and none of the reschedule, unschedule, share or cancel actions a content item has. A **Calendar alerts panel under the grid** lists every alert with Open, Due soon, Snoozed, Done and All filters and adds, edits, finishes, snoozes and deletes them; a change in the panel makes the grid read again and a change from a chip reloads the panel. **Download .ics** builds a calendar file in the browser and saves it to the owner's disk, so it has no web address. On sign-in an editor or above sees a dialog (focus goes to the dialog, not to a button; focus kept inside it; **Esc** closes it; role `dialog`) listing every open alert due within 7 days or overdue, each with Done, Snooze (1 day, 3 days, next week) and Open link; it opens at most once per browser session and once per UTC day, only inside the admin layout, and never blocks sign-in: a failed read shows a small notice with Try again, and a failure to even load the pop-up renders nothing. Backend: `GET` and `POST` `cms/calendar-alerts` and `PATCH` and `DELETE` `cms/calendar-alerts/{alertId}` (`functions/src/lib/calendar-alerts/`), editor and above, registered in `function-inventory.json` and `.azure/api-surface.json`. **The alerts keep their own store, one document `admin_config/calendar_alerts` (no new container), and not a content or social record, because the Calendar owns no storage and the records it shows are the ones the scheduled publisher (`scheduledPublishDate`), the Publer sync (`scheduledAt`) and the newsletter send act on: an alert stored as one could be published or posted.** It is written under its ETag with a retry on a lost race, and is read by no public route, the content manifest, the prerender, the sitemap, the newsletter or the social queue. **The starting alert is made by the server on the first list read after the deploy, create-only under the fixed id `docker-dsos-application`, with the ids of every alert ever made recorded in the same document, so a second read changes nothing and an alert marked done or deleted is never made again** (the Calendar read adds it in memory, writing nothing, if it is read first). Titles, notes and links are never logged, and the audit row holds the alert id, its state and, for an edit, the names of the fields changed, never their values. Links are printable ASCII only and may not point at an OAuth route; the link button names the site it goes to; a stored row is checked again on the way out, and the .ics builder drops control characters and the other line-end characters so no title or note can add a calendar property. Runbook: [Calendar Alerts](docs/runbooks/calendar-alerts.md). Separate on purpose from the Telegram reminders sheet. Landed in [#1390](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1390).

### Quality & Verification

- **A CI job whose filter `grep` cannot read now fails loudly instead of being switched off, and the filter guard now runs on every pull request ([#1428](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1428)).** Two follow-ups to [#1427](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1427). *First,* each job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` decides whether a pull request needs it by running `grep -E` with the job's `filter` (a pattern for file paths) over the files the pull request changes. `grep` answers 0 (a file matches), 1 (none does) or 2 (it could not read the pattern, for example because a parenthesis is never closed). The four change-detection steps (the `verify` matrix, `ansible-lint (lab-host)`, `coder (lab-host)` and `harness (python)`) tested that answer with `if grep ...`, which treats 2 like 1, so a broken filter would have skipped its job as "no relevant change" and left the pull request looking green. The steps now keep the answer: 0 writes `relevant=true`, 1 writes `relevant=false`, and anything else fails the step with a message that names the job and the filter. A diff that cannot be computed still runs everything, as before. The three steps that kept their pattern inside the script now take it from a `FILTER` setting like the matrix step, so the lines that decide are the same in all four, and the filter is put in brackets before `ci.yml` is added to it, so a stray backslash at the end of a filter cannot join onto the `|` and hide the mistake. The new `scripts/ci-workflow-steps.test.mjs` takes each step's shell out of `ci.yml` and runs it with bash in a temporary git repository (a matching file, a file that does not match, three filters `grep` cannot read, `ci.yml` itself, a base commit that cannot be fetched, a push to `main`); on the old `ci.yml` 20 of its tests fail, the broken filter ending with exit code 0 and `relevant=false`. *Second,* the guard (`scripts/ci-filters.test.mjs`) lives in the scripts package, so it ran only when the `scripts (operations)` row ran, and a pull request that changed only a frontend or functions test first met it on `main` after the merge. A new step, "CI path filters list every file the tests read", runs it on every pull request, outside the filter, like the two checks beside it (`oidc-subjects.test.mjs` is the model), and the scripts row now installs its packages on every pull request so the step can run; the same new test file keeps the step outside the filter and works out which steps each row runs for a pull request that changes only `frontend/src/x.test.jsx`. Replayed over the last 150 merged commits on `main`, the guard ran for 141 (94%) before and runs for all 150 now; adding the other packages' test files to the row's filter would have reached 143 and adding their folders whole 145, and both keep a list that someone has to keep up by hand. On the runner, in this change's own CI run, the install took 5 seconds and the new step 12 (about 15 seconds for the guard on its own on the machine it was first timed on), and the scripts row is not on the longest path: on the last run on `main` `scripts (operations)` took 53 seconds and `frontend` 165. `codeql.yml` and `iac-validate.yml` still use the `if grep` shape and are not changed here ([#1429](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1429) tracks them). Decision record: [0026](docs/decisions/0026-required-checks-filter-inside-the-job.md).

- **The Doc Vault "linear time" test no longer fails by chance ([#1431](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1431)).** The test (`functions/src/lib/doc-vault/markdown.test.js`, group "linear time") checks that the reader for uploaded Markdown files takes about four times as long for four times as much text, not sixteen times, which would mean the reader had become *quadratic* (slower and slower as the text grows, so one big file could keep the server busy). It does that by timing the reader with a clock. On 2026-10-27 it failed in [CI run 40484952326](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/actions/runs/40484952326) with a ratio of 11.9 (the limit is 9) on a pull request that changed only documentation, so the cause was timing noise on the shared test machine and not the reader. The failure could not be repeated here (0 failures in 300 runs of the file on an idle machine and in 100 runs with 48 busy programs running beside it), so the cause was read from the timings instead. The large input was timed as five single parses of about a tenth to a quarter of a millisecond each, all inside about two milliseconds. Across 8,144 local readings of the old measurement the ratio of the four shapes that do real work was normally 3.5 to 4.1 and reached 6.9 at most; in the worst cases whose individual timings were recorded (ratios of 5.8 and 6.3), all five large timings were slow together (1.6 to 1.9 times their usual) and the small timings, taken earlier, could not cancel that. Three of the eight shapes also sat under a floor of 0.02 ms that was 3 to 14 times their real time (0.0014 to 0.007 ms), so their growth was never measured. Now every timing repeats the parse until it lasts at least 4 ms, the small and large inputs are timed in alternating rounds so a slow moment lands on both and cancels out, each keeps its fastest of nine rounds, and the floor is gone. The check is still the ratio, still under 9, on the same eight shapes, and a failure now prints both timings. Measured side by side in one process on an idle machine (2,000 readings each): the highest ratio fell from 5.04 to 4.25, and the gap between the median and the 99th percentile for the four shapes that do real work fell from 0.58 to 0.29. It still has teeth: against a reader made quadratic on purpose (a temporary local change, not committed) the old and the new test both fail on all eight shapes when the slowdown follows the text length, and on exactly the shapes a slowdown touches when it follows the line count (3), a value's length (4) or a heading's length (1); for a mild slowdown (1/1,024, 1/16,384 and 1/262,144 of that cost) the new test fails on 6, 3 and 1 shapes against 4, 2 and 0 for the old one. The price is time: the group takes about 1.0 s instead of 0.06 s on an idle machine, and 2.9 s instead of 0.26 s with the busy programs. Not verified: Node 24 (CI's version; this machine has 26.5) and a CI run. The same timing method in `frontend/src/pages/admin/docVault/docVaultModel.test.js` (the plain-text converter) has the same weakness and is not changed here.

- **The CI path-filter guard now works out which files a test reads, so a read written with `join(...)` can no longer slip past it ([#1414](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/issues/1414)).** Each test job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on a pull request only when the pull request changes a file its `filter` matches, and `scripts/ci-filters.test.mjs` fails when a test reads a file outside its package that the filter misses. The first version cut each read off at its first comma, so `readFileSync(join(HERE, '..', 'functions', 'x.js'))` was read as `join(HERE` and dropped, which is how the Cloud Crawler registry file was missed in [#1413](https://github.com/saulpatinojr/HCW-HybridCloudWorks/pull/1413). `scripts/lib/js-file-reads.mjs` now parses the test with `espree` (the parser ESLint already uses; it becomes a direct dev dependency of `scripts/`) and follows `join`, `resolve`, `new URL`, variables, loops and helper functions, including helpers in other files. A read it cannot follow, or a use of the file functions it cannot see through, fails the test instead of being skipped; the only way past is a reason written in `REVIEWED_READS`, and an entry that no longer matches a read fails too. Run against `main`'s filters it reports 40 gaps: 33 files and 4 folders that tests read, and 3 `.nvmrc` files that the version-floors checks read. The filters now cover them. `functions (azure)` also runs for any change under `frontend/src/`, `frontend/scripts/`, `frontend/public/` and `scripts/`, because the Doc Vault test reads every source file in them: over the last 150 merged pull requests it would have run on 111 instead of 66, `frontend` on 67 instead of 64, and `scripts (operations)` on the same 141. What the guard still cannot see is listed at the top of the test.

- **CI now runs `npm run validate:routes` on every pull request that touches
  the frontend (#1345)**. The validator fails when a page spells a provider
  path by hand (`href="/azure/..."`) instead of building it from the route
  factory, which stays correct until a route is renamed and then breaks that
  page silently. It was not run by CI, so #1337 merged two such paths and only
  a hand run found them (fixed in #1338). It is a new *Route validation* step
  in the frontend row of `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, after *Format check*,
  switched on by a `validate` key on that row so no other package runs it.
  Seen both ways locally: exit 0 on the current tree, and exit 1 with the file
  and the path named when a component with a hard-coded `href="/azure/..."`
  was planted, then removed. Not yet seen in a CI run; this pull request's own
  frontend job is the first.
- **The AVM versions bot's check step reads the pins instead of remembering

### Security

- **Sign-in library `@azure/msal-node` forced to 7.1.1 in `functions`,
  `scripts` and `vps-agent`, closing three High Dependabot alerts (#163, #164,
  #165)**. Owner decision 2026-10-24. The alerts are for
  [GHSA-xcx6-jx8p-x3h5](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xcx6-jx8p-x3h5)
  (CVSS 7.5): in msal-node's authorization-code flow, parameters can be sent to
  an attacker-controlled endpoint; fixed in 7.1.0. `@azure/identity` 4.14.0,
  which pulls the library in, still asks for `^6.0.0`, so Dependabot could not
  fix it by itself; an npm `overrides` entry in each `package.json` now makes
  every copy 7.1.1. Before opening this, the managed-identity path (the one the
  Function App uses for Cosmos, Blob and Key Vault) was run against a stand-in
  for the App Service identity endpoint on 6.0.1 and again on 7.1.1, in all
  three packages: the same six checks passed both times (system-assigned and
  client-id tokens, the token cache, concurrent calls, `DefaultAzureCredential`,
  and a refused request). All three test suites pass. **Not tested:** the real
  Azure endpoint, Azure Arc on the lab host, and the workload-identity login in
  CI; the owner deploys the functions and watches the delivery monitor. The
  override is recorded as an accepted risk in `TODO.md` with its removal
  trigger.
- **Coder rotation credential: measured, and kept unscoped with the reason (#1037)**.
  On the live Coder 2.38.0 on 2026-10-19, with throwaway tokens of
  `hcw-status`: a token with `coder:templates.author`, `organization:read`
  and `user:read` publishes the template and cannot mint keys; a token with
  `api_key:create` and `user:read` mints tokens with scopes it does not hold
  and those tokens use them, so the inheritance rule in Coder's current docs
  is not enforced on this version; scopes are enforced on reads by filtering
  (`workspace:read` alone sees no templates), and an out-of-scope write
  answers 500 rather than 403. Since any credential that renews the status
  token can mint any scope, narrowing the rotation credential contains
  nothing against a leak; it stays `coder:all` and containment stays on the
  account. The results are the second table under "The status token for the
  site" in `lab-host/README.md`; the role README and the runbook point at it.
  Three tokens of `hcw-status` that nothing held (two hand-made status tokens
  superseded on 2026-10-10, and the old host's rotation credential restored
  by the snapshot) were deleted.
- **LAB-9 rebuild rehearsal done on the live lab host: 66 min 42 s (#955)**.
  2026-10-18, VM 939861 recreated through Hostinger's API on the same plain
  Ubuntu 26.04 template; Vault unsealed on the snapshot's data 66 min 42 s
  after the click, Coder back on the restored database at 58 min. The
  runbook's "Reinstalling the host" step 7 is rewritten in the order the
  rehearsal proved: the nine vault keys set by hand (three add-on Turnstile
  secrets, not one), Arc's two runs and then `Connect-Lab.ps1 -Arc` before
  any further play (the post-onboarding run closes port 22), the `hcw-azure`
  run for the new machine identity, `bootstrap.sh --skip-tags coder` (Coder's
  first account cannot be made by password on this build, and the restore
  brings the accounts back), the Coder restore, the seal check, the agent
